assignment-v2.welcome: Let’s get your lab organized before we build anything. We’ll make a small notebook and choose names for the Linux computer you’ll use throughout the course.
assignment-v2.why: Think of the notebook as our map. It helps you find the right computer later and remember what worked before a change.
needs: You’ll need your own Windows computer and a place to save a plain-text notes file.
Have Windows Terminal or Windows PowerShell available; we’ll check the rest of the tools next.
Use the name rexuser for the Linux administrator in this lab. We are only writing down that name for now.
assignment-v2.firstMove: On Windows, open Notepad and save a new file as your lab notes. Then open Windows Terminal and choose PowerShell.
assignment-v2.reassurance: You don’t need a Linux computer yet. If Azure account details are still unknown, leave them blank rather than guessing.

windows-tools-v2.welcome: Before we connect to Linux, let’s check the tools on your Windows computer. We’ll meet the sign-in tool, two file-copy tools, and the tool that makes our sign-in keys.
windows-tools-v2.why: Using the right tool makes the job easier: SSH opens a remote command window, while SCP and SFTP move files.
needs: You’ll need the same Windows computer you used for your lab notes.
Open Windows Terminal and select PowerShell, or open Windows PowerShell from Start.
Keep your notes nearby so you can record which tools are present.
windows-tools-v2.firstMove: Click Start, type Windows Terminal, open it, and choose the PowerShell tab. We’ll run the tool check there.
windows-tools-v2.reassurance: A missing tool is something we can fix. Read its name in the result; you don’t need to rebuild your computer.

azure-scope-v2.welcome: Let’s make sure Azure is using the right account before we spend any money. We’ll find your subscription, choose a region, and write down a small lab budget.
azure-scope-v2.why: An Azure subscription is the account that pays for the lab. Picking it carefully prevents surprises on somebody else’s bill.
needs: You’ll need an Azure account and a subscription you are allowed to use for practice.
Keep a browser and your Windows PowerShell tab open.
Have your lab notes ready for the subscription name, region, spending limit, and person to contact about charges.
azure-scope-v2.firstMove: Open portal.azure.com in your browser. Sign in, then search for Subscriptions and check the account shown.
azure-scope-v2.reassurance: If you can’t tell which subscription to use, pause here and check with its owner. There is nothing to create yet.

two-host-plan-v3.welcome: Our lab will have two Linux computers with different jobs. We’ll keep rhel9-lab-01 as the endpoint and plan rhel9-manager-01 as the computer that receives its security information.
two-host-plan-v3.why: The manager stores and displays information, so it needs more resources than the small program on the endpoint. Giving both the same small size can make the manager struggle.
needs: You’ll need your existing endpoint plan and the Azure subscription and region you checked earlier.
For the Wazuh manager, plan at least 4 virtual CPU cores, 8 GiB of memory, and 50 GB of storage, or more if the selected image requires it.
Keep one row per computer in your notes, with its name, job, addresses, size, and expected cost.
two-host-plan-v3.firstMove: Open your lab notebook and add two rows: rhel9-lab-01 for the endpoint and rhel9-manager-01 for the manager.
two-host-plan-v3.reassurance: If your budget can’t support the manager’s required size, stop and adjust the plan before creating it. A smaller machine is not automatically a working substitute.

resource-group-v2.welcome: Now let’s give our Azure lab a home. We’ll create rg-rhel9-lab, a resource group that keeps the lab’s related items together.
resource-group-v2.why: A resource group is like a labeled project folder. It makes things easier to find, but deleting it can also delete the resources inside.
needs: You’ll need the Azure subscription and region you selected in the previous lesson.
Keep your browser signed in to portal.azure.com.
Have your lab notes open so you can record the resource group’s actual name and location.
resource-group-v2.firstMove: In Azure, search for Resource groups, open it, and select Create.
resource-group-v2.reassurance: If the name already belongs to another project, don’t reuse it blindly. Check what it contains and confirm your own lab’s name first.

network-plan-v2.welcome: Let’s build the private network our two Linux computers will share. We’ll create vnet-rhel9-lab and a smaller address section inside it called snet-rhel9-lab.
network-plan-v2.why: A virtual network, or VNet, lets our Azure computers talk to each other. A subnet gives us a smaller address range to organize them.
needs: You’ll need the empty rg-rhel9-lab resource group from the previous lesson.
Use the same Azure subscription and region recorded in your notes.
Check that the example address ranges do not overlap another network you need to connect to.
network-plan-v2.firstMove: In the Azure search bar, type Virtual networks, open the service, and select Create.
network-plan-v2.reassurance: If an address range overlaps another network, stop and ask for a suitable range. Changing random numbers can create a harder problem later.

build-storage-v3.welcome: Before clicking Create on a VM, let’s look at where its files will live. We’ll choose the operating-system disks and learn what Linux means by a mount point.
build-storage-v3.why: Disk space can fill up. Knowing which disk holds which files helps us size the lab and understand storage problems later.
needs: You’ll need the endpoint and manager size plans you already wrote down.
Keep the Azure VM creation form and your lab notebook open.
Remember that the Wazuh manager needs at least the supported storage capacity; the chosen image may require a larger operating-system disk.
build-storage-v3.firstMove: Open the VM creation form’s Disks tab and read the operating-system disk size before changing any option.
build-storage-v3.reassurance: This is a planning step. You don’t need to partition an existing disk or add a data disk just to finish it.

nsg-v2.welcome: Let’s open the right network door for your home computer. We’ll allow its current internet address to reach SSH, the secure sign-in connection on port 22.
nsg-v2.why: The Azure network rule controls who can reach the sign-in door. Your username and key will still decide who can actually sign in.
needs: You’ll need your Windows computer, a browser signed in to the correct Azure account, and your network plan.
Find the public IPv4 address your home connection is using today; it can change.
Have the endpoint’s network security group, or NSG, ready. An NSG is Azure’s list of allowed and blocked network traffic.
nsg-v2.firstMove: On your own Windows computer, open portal.azure.com and find the network security group for your endpoint lab network.
nsg-v2.reassurance: If SSH still fails later, that doesn’t mean the rule is wrong. We’ll check the network connection and the sign-in key separately.

key-concept-v2.welcome: Before we make a key, let’s understand its two parts. The private key stays on your Windows computer; its public partner goes to Linux.
key-concept-v2.why: The pair helps prove it is you signing in. The private key should never be pasted into Azure, a screenshot, or a class note.
needs: You’ll need Windows PowerShell and your lab notes.
We’ll use a folder named .ssh inside your own Windows user folder.
Keep existing keys safe. This lesson chooses file paths; it does not create or replace a key.
key-concept-v2.firstMove: Open your Windows PowerShell tab and read the three example key paths before setting their values.
key-concept-v2.reassurance: The similar filenames can be confusing at first. Look for .pub: that is the public file, not the private one.

key-create-v2.welcome: Let’s create your sign-in key pair carefully. We’ll check for existing files first, then protect the new private key with a passphrase.
key-create-v2.why: Overwriting a working private key can lock you out of a computer. Our checks help keep the keys you already use safe.
needs: You’ll need the .ssh folder and key paths planned in the previous lesson.
Use your own Windows PowerShell tab and normal Windows account.
Have a password manager or other approved private place ready for your key’s passphrase.
key-create-v2.firstMove: In PowerShell, check the planned private and public filenames with Test-Path before running ssh-keygen.
key-create-v2.reassurance: If either file already exists, stop. We can check the existing key or choose a new filename; we don’t have to replace it.

vm-provision-v2.welcome: You’re ready to create the endpoint Linux computer. We’ll build rhel9-lab-01 in Azure and give the rexuser account your public key.
vm-provision-v2.why: The public key tells the new VM which sign-in proof to accept. Keeping the private partner on Windows protects your access.
needs: You’ll need your checked Azure subscription, resource group, network, region, and endpoint size plan.
Have your rexuser public key file ending in .pub ready; keep the private file on Windows.
Choose a supported x64 RHEL 9 image and check the cost shown before creating the VM.
vm-provision-v2.firstMove: In Azure, search for Virtual machines and choose Create → Azure virtual machine.
vm-provision-v2.reassurance: If the form asks for a key, use only the .pub file’s text. If you can’t tell which file is which, return to the key lesson before continuing.

manager-vm-v3.welcome: Now we’ll add the manager without losing the endpoint you already built. Its name is rhel9-manager-01, and we’ll keep separate notes for both computers.
manager-vm-v3.why: Two similar VM screens are easy to mix up. Clear names and separate address rows help us install the central tools on the right machine.
needs: You’ll need the working rhel9-lab-01 endpoint and your existing network and key notes.
Choose a supported RHEL 9 x64 manager VM with at least 4 virtual CPU cores, 8 GiB of memory, and 50 GB of storage, or the image’s larger minimum.
Leave room in your budget for both VMs and their retained disks and addresses.
manager-vm-v3.firstMove: Open Virtual machines in Azure, confirm that rhel9-lab-01 is still present, then start a new VM creation form for rhel9-manager-01.
manager-vm-v3.reassurance: If both machines appear with similar addresses, slow down and label each row. A public address is for this lab’s Windows sign-in; the private address is for traffic between the VMs.

reachability-v2.welcome: Before trying a password or key, let’s see whether Windows can reach the VM’s SSH connection. This is a small network check, not a sign-in attempt.
reachability-v2.why: Separating the two jobs makes troubleshooting easier. A network failure needs a different fix from a rejected key.
needs: You’ll need a running endpoint VM and its actual public IPv4 address from Azure.
Keep Windows PowerShell open on the computer allowed by your SSH network rule.
Check your current home public address if you changed networks since creating that rule.
reachability-v2.firstMove: Open the endpoint’s Overview page in Azure and copy its current public IPv4 address into your notes.
reachability-v2.reassurance: If the port test fails, keep the result. We’ll check the VM, network rule, and route before changing any sign-in files.

host-trust-v2.welcome: Let’s check the Linux computer’s identity before we trust a new connection. We’ll read its SSH fingerprint through Azure and save the exact value.
host-trust-v2.why: A fingerprint is a short identifying value for a key. Comparing it helps us avoid signing in to the wrong computer.
needs: You’ll need the running rhel9-lab-01 endpoint and permission to use its Azure Run Command page.
Have your lab notebook ready to save the exact SHA256 fingerprint.
Remember that this is the server’s host key, not the rexuser key you created on Windows.
host-trust-v2.firstMove: Open rhel9-lab-01 in Azure, choose Run command, then select RunShellScript.
host-trust-v2.reassurance: If the offered key type later differs from the one you recorded, don’t accept it by habit. Obtain the matching host-key fingerprint first.

first-ssh-v2.welcome: Let’s make your first secure sign-in to the endpoint. We’ll connect from Windows as rexuser and compare the computer’s fingerprint before accepting it.
first-ssh-v2.why: SSH protects the connection, but we still need to check both sides: which server we reached and which account we’re using.
needs: You’ll need the endpoint’s actual public address and a successful port 22 connection test.
Have your existing private-key path and its passphrase ready on Windows.
Keep the independently recorded server fingerprint beside you for comparison.
first-ssh-v2.firstMove: Return to your Windows PowerShell tab and check that $VmAddress and $KeyPath match your saved endpoint notes.
first-ssh-v2.reassurance: A passphrase prompt may show no typed characters. That is normal. If the fingerprint differs, stop and investigate instead of typing yes.

identity-v2.welcome: You’re inside Linux. Before changing anything, let’s check your username and the extra permissions you’re allowed to use.
identity-v2.why: A command can affect the wrong account or computer if we skip this check. sudo gives an allowed user extra rights for a particular command.
needs: You’ll need the verified SSH session to rhel9-lab-01, signed in as rexuser.
Keep the Linux prompt visible; the commands in this lesson are not for your local PowerShell tab.
Have the account’s configured password available privately if sudo asks for it.
identity-v2.firstMove: Select the endpoint’s connected SSH tab and run whoami to read the current username.
identity-v2.reassurance: If the name isn’t rexuser, pause and check which session you opened. You can correct the connection before making changes.

host-os-v2.welcome: Let’s get to know this Linux computer. We’ll read its name, RHEL release, and the kernel it is running.
host-os-v2.why: The kernel is the core part of Linux. Knowing the actual version helps us choose instructions and updates that fit this computer.
needs: You’ll need your verified rexuser SSH session on rhel9-lab-01.
Keep your endpoint row in the notebook open so you can add its release and kernel.
Use the Linux terminal for these checks; no software installation is needed.
host-os-v2.firstMove: In the endpoint SSH tab, run hostnamectl and compare the computer name with your notes.
host-os-v2.reassurance: Different release numbers are useful clues. Record what you actually see and check compatibility before following version-specific instructions.

guest-network-v2.welcome: Now let’s look at the network from inside Linux. We’ll find the endpoint’s private address and the path it uses to reach other networks.
guest-network-v2.why: Azure shows a public sign-in address, but Linux usually sees its private interface address. They have different jobs and do not need to match.
needs: You’ll need your working endpoint SSH session as rexuser.
Have the endpoint’s private and public Azure addresses recorded separately.
Keep the Azure network page available for comparison; this lesson only reads settings.
guest-network-v2.firstMove: In the endpoint’s Linux terminal, run the address check and find the interface with the lab’s private IPv4 address.
guest-network-v2.reassurance: Don’t copy the public Azure address into Linux’s interface settings. If the addresses are confusing, compare each one with its labeled row first.

home-files-v2.welcome: Let’s find your Linux home folder and see the public key that allows you to sign in. We’ll look before we change any files.
home-files-v2.why: Your home folder stores your own files. Knowing where you are makes later copying and permission changes much easier.
needs: You’ll need the endpoint SSH session, signed in as rexuser.
Keep the public-key lesson’s notes available so the filenames look familiar.
We are inspecting the account’s files, not opening or copying your Windows private key.
home-files-v2.firstMove: In the endpoint terminal, run pwd to see your current folder, then use the lesson’s home-folder checks.
home-files-v2.reassurance: A filename starting with a dot is usually hidden in normal listings. That is why we use the option that shows hidden files too.

storage-verify-v3.welcome: Let’s check the storage we actually built instead of relying on the plan. We’ll read the disks, their mount points, and the free space on each VM.
storage-verify-v3.why: A mount point is the folder where Linux makes a disk’s files available. This check helps us notice a nearly full disk before an installation fails.
needs: You’ll need verified rexuser access to both the endpoint and manager.
Have each VM’s disk plan in your notebook.
Keep the terminal tabs clearly labeled; record one computer’s results before moving to the other.
storage-verify-v3.firstMove: Select one VM’s SSH tab and run hostname before reading its disk information.
storage-verify-v3.reassurance: Disk names and sizes can differ from examples. Write down your real results; do not format or resize anything to make the screen look the same.

paired-access-v3.welcome: Let’s prove you can reach both Linux computers and tell them apart. We’ll sign in to the manager, then compare the names in our two terminal tabs.
paired-access-v3.why: Once installation begins, running a correct command on the wrong VM can still cause trouble. Clear session labels prevent that mix-up.
needs: You’ll need both Azure VMs running and both public sign-in addresses in your notes.
Have the existing rexuser private key and its passphrase ready on Windows.
Verify each server’s host fingerprint through its own Azure page before accepting a new SSH connection.
paired-access-v3.firstMove: In Windows Terminal, open a second PowerShell tab and label it for rhel9-manager-01 before connecting.
paired-access-v3.reassurance: If you lose track of a tab, run hostname and whoami inside it. Those two quick checks tell you where you are.

test-file-v3.welcome: Let’s make a tiny text file we can safely copy between computers. We’ll also calculate a checksum, a value that helps us check the file’s contents later.
test-file-v3.why: A harmless practice file lets us learn file transfer without risking personal documents or software installers.
needs: You’ll need your own Windows PowerShell tab and user folder.
Keep the notebook ready for the practice filename and its SHA-256 checksum.
Choose the new practice filename from the lesson; don’t replace a file containing work you need.
test-file-v3.firstMove: On Windows, open your user folder in PowerShell and check whether rexuser-transfer-v3.txt already exists.
test-file-v3.reassurance: If the filename already contains useful work, keep it. We can choose a separate practice file instead of overwriting it.

scp-test-v3.welcome: Let’s send the practice file from Windows to the endpoint. SCP copies a file through the same secure connection used by SSH.
scp-test-v3.why: This is how an administrator can deliver a small file while keeping the source and destination clear.
needs: You’ll need rexuser-transfer-v3.txt in your Windows user folder from the previous lesson.
Have the endpoint’s actual public address, your existing private-key path, and a working SSH connection.
Use the local Windows PowerShell tab for the copy command, not the remote Linux tab.
scp-test-v3.firstMove: In Windows PowerShell, move to your user folder and check that the practice file is present.
scp-test-v3.reassurance: If SCP says it cannot find the file, check the Windows folder first. Recreating your SSH key will not fix a missing local file.

verify-transfer-v3.welcome: The copy finished, but let’s make sure the right file arrived. We’ll check it on Linux and compare its checksum with the one recorded on Windows.
verify-transfer-v3.why: A matching filename alone does not prove the contents are right. Comparing checksums gives us a stronger check.
needs: You’ll need the practice file already copied to rhel9-lab-01.
Have your endpoint SSH session open as rexuser.
Keep the original Windows SHA-256 value in your notes for an exact comparison.
verify-transfer-v3.firstMove: Select the endpoint’s Linux terminal, confirm its name, and list the received practice file in rexuser’s home folder.
verify-transfer-v3.reassurance: If the values differ, keep both results and recopy the intended file. Don’t edit the recorded checksum to make it match.

sftp-test-v3.welcome: Now let’s try a different way to move that same practice file. SFTP gives you a file-transfer prompt where you can look around and choose what to copy.
sftp-test-v3.why: It helps you understand which folder is on Windows and which folder is on Linux before sending a file.
needs: You’ll need the same harmless Windows practice file and a working endpoint SSH connection.
Have the endpoint address and existing private-key path ready.
Use a local Windows PowerShell tab; we’ll start the SFTP tool there.
sftp-test-v3.firstMove: In Windows PowerShell, open your user folder and confirm the practice file exists before starting SFTP.
sftp-test-v3.reassurance: At the sftp prompt, local and remote folders are different. If a file seems missing, check which side you are listing before trying again.

installer-types-v3.welcome: Before we install real software, let’s sort out three common file types: scripts, RPM packages, and compressed archives. They are not all installed the same way.
installer-types-v3.why: Giving a file permission to run does not install it or make it trustworthy. Learning the difference helps you avoid unsafe guesses.
needs: You’ll need your notes and the reference examples in this lesson.
No download or software installation is required for these commented examples.
Remember that a line beginning with # is a comment here, so the examples explain methods without running them.
installer-types-v3.firstMove: Read the first script example and point out the # at the beginning of each sample line.
installer-types-v3.reassurance: You don’t have to memorize every option today. Start by saying whether a command inspects, extracts, changes a permission, or installs software.

software-inventory-v3.welcome: Let’s take a before picture of the software and services on each VM. We’ll save the lists so we can see what the Wazuh installation changes.
software-inventory-v3.why: A service is a program that can keep running in the background. Before-and-after lists make missing or unexpected changes easier to find.
needs: You’ll need rexuser access to the endpoint and manager.
Keep separate note sections for rhel9-lab-01 and rhel9-manager-01.
Use the Linux terminal for these read-only checks; no new package is being installed yet.
software-inventory-v3.firstMove: Choose one VM, run hostname, and save its installed-package list under that computer’s name.
software-inventory-v3.reassurance: The lists can be long. You don’t need to understand every package name; you’re saving a record we can compare later.

baseline-v2.welcome: Before installing Wazuh, let’s check that Linux is working normally. We’ll record the SSH service, free space, security mode, and administrator access.
baseline-v2.why: This working starting point is called a baseline. If something changes later, we’ll have real results to compare against.
needs: You’ll need your verified rexuser SSH session on the endpoint.
Have the earlier software and storage notes available.
Keep the account’s configured password private if sudo asks for it.
baseline-v2.firstMove: In the endpoint SSH tab, check that the SSH service is active before moving to the other starting point checks.
baseline-v2.reassurance: If a starting check fails, it’s useful that we found it now. Resolve it before adding more software.

rollback-gate-v3.welcome: Let’s decide how to get back to a working computer before the next change. We’ll write down what needs protection, how to restore it, and when we would stop.
rollback-gate-v3.why: A snapshot is a point-in-time disk copy, not a complete recovery plan. We also need the right disks, a way to sign in, and checks that prove recovery worked.
needs: You’ll need the working starting point and the names of both lab VMs.
Have access to the chosen backup or snapshot controls and know which disks hold the files you need.
Write down a restore method and stop condition before changing the computer; protect important data independently.
rollback-gate-v3.firstMove: Open your notes and add three headings: What we’ll protect, How we’ll recover, and When we’ll stop.
rollback-gate-v3.reassurance: If you can’t explain the restore steps yet, pause here. It’s much easier to learn recovery while the original computer still works.

deallocate-v2.welcome: Let’s finish the session without accidentally leaving a VM running. We’ll leave Linux, then stop both computers through Azure.
deallocate-v2.why: Closing a terminal is like closing a window: the computer behind it keeps running. Azure must show Stopped (deallocated) to release the running compute allocation.
needs: You’ll need access to both VM pages in the Azure Portal.
Save any files and finish important tasks before stopping the VMs.
Keep your notes ready for the final power states and any disks, addresses, or recovery copies that still have charges.
deallocate-v2.firstMove: Save your work in Linux and type exit in the SSH tab to return to Windows PowerShell.
deallocate-v2.reassurance: If Azure says only Stopped, check again for the deallocated state. Don’t delete disks or the resource group just to end today’s session.

wazuh-release-v4.welcome: We’re nearly ready to install Wazuh. First, let’s check that the release, manager size, and recovery copies match the plan we made.
wazuh-release-v4.why: The manager runs several tools together. Checking its resources and supported release now can prevent a confusing half-finished installation.
needs: You’ll need rhel9-manager-01 and rhel9-lab-01 running, with their four public/private addresses recorded separately.
The manager needs at least 4 virtual CPU cores, 8 GiB of memory, and 50 GB of storage, or the image’s larger minimum.
Have your working starting point, retained recovery copies, and official release notes ready; this course’s Wazuh release checkpoint is 4.14.7.
wazuh-release-v4.firstMove: Open Virtual machines in Azure and check the name, resource group, and Running status of rhel9-manager-01.
wazuh-release-v4.reassurance: If current release guidance differs from the course checkpoint, pause and compare it before installing. Don’t mix instructions from different releases.

wazuh-central-v4.welcome: Let’s install the central Wazuh tools on the manager. We’ll check the downloaded installer first, then follow the installation and keep its private output safe.
wazuh-central-v4.why: The manager receives information, the indexer stores and searches it, and the dashboard lets you read it in a browser. These belong on the manager VM, not the endpoint.
needs: You’ll need the approved release checkpoint, a tested recovery plan, and the adequately sized rhel9-manager-01 VM.
Open its verified SSH session as rexuser and keep the endpoint’s tab separate.
Have private storage ready for generated credentials and recovery files; do not put them in screenshots or GitHub.
wazuh-central-v4.firstMove: Select the manager’s SSH tab and run whoami, hostname, and pwd one at a time.
wazuh-central-v4.reassurance: If the computer name is wrong, stop before downloading or running the installer. Picking the right tab is part of doing this well.

wazuh-dashboard-v4.welcome: The central tools are installed. Now let’s check their services and open the Wazuh dashboard from Windows.
wazuh-dashboard-v4.why: An installer finishing doesn’t prove that the services or browser connection work. We’ll test them in small, separate steps.
needs: You’ll need the completed central installation on rhel9-manager-01.
Keep its SSH tab and the Windows browser available, along with the private dashboard credentials.
Know the manager’s public address for browser access and your current home public address for the restricted dashboard rule.
wazuh-dashboard-v4.firstMove: Select the manager SSH tab, confirm its name, and check the installed service information before opening the browser.
wazuh-dashboard-v4.reassurance: If the page doesn’t load, work from the service to the listening port and then the network rule. Reinstalling everything is not our first move.

wazuh-artifact-v4.welcome: Let’s get the endpoint’s Wazuh agent package and check it before installation. We’ll compare the file’s details and publisher signature with the official source.
wazuh-artifact-v4.why: A file with the right name can still be wrong. These checks help us avoid installing a damaged or untrusted package.
needs: You’ll need the approved Wazuh release and its official x86_64 agent-package source.
Open the verified rexuser SSH session on rhel9-lab-01, not on the manager.
Keep the official package checks and trusted signing-key guidance available for comparison.
wazuh-artifact-v4.firstMove: In the endpoint’s SSH tab, run whoami and hostname to confirm rexuser on rhel9-lab-01.
wazuh-artifact-v4.reassurance: If a signature or checksum check fails, keep the result and stop. A failed trust check is not something to skip to make the install continue.

wazuh-agent-v4.welcome: Now we’ll install the small Wazuh agent on the endpoint and tell it how to reach the manager over the private network.
wazuh-agent-v4.why: The agent sends the endpoint’s security information to the manager. Using the correct private address keeps that traffic on the intended path.
needs: You’ll need the verified agent RPM already saved on rhel9-lab-01.
Have the manager’s actual private address from your notes, with the manager services ready.
Use the endpoint SSH session as rexuser and the reviewed private-network rules for agent traffic.
wazuh-agent-v4.firstMove: Select the endpoint SSH tab and confirm the username and computer name before opening its sonic-wazuh folder.
wazuh-agent-v4.reassurance: If the agent installs but doesn’t connect, check its configured manager address and logs. Running and connected are two different checks.

wazuh-checkin-v4.welcome: Let’s find your endpoint in the dashboard and prove it is the same computer we configured. We’ll compare its name, agent ID, and recent activity.
wazuh-checkin-v4.why: A green symbol beside another computer does not prove our lab is connected. Matching identities and recent information gives us better evidence.
needs: You’ll need the installed agent on rhel9-lab-01 and the working manager dashboard.
Keep the endpoint SSH session and dashboard open side by side if possible.
Have your recorded host names and private addresses available so you can identify the correct entry.
wazuh-checkin-v4.firstMove: In the endpoint terminal, read its hostname and current time before comparing its agent details with the dashboard.
wazuh-checkin-v4.reassurance: If there are duplicate names, don’t choose the green one by guesswork. Compare the agent ID and the latest activity too.

wazuh-event-v4.welcome: Let’s watch a harmless file change travel from Linux into Wazuh. We’ll use a small practice folder, not a system file or personal document.
wazuh-event-v4.why: Finding the actual event shows that the connection carries useful information, not just that a service happens to be running.
needs: You’ll need the endpoint checking in successfully and the manager dashboard available.
Use the verified rexuser endpoint session and the dedicated sonic-fim practice folder.
Keep a backup of the agent configuration before adding the reviewed file-monitoring setting.
wazuh-event-v4.firstMove: Confirm you are on rhel9-lab-01, then create the harmless practice folder and starting point text file from the lesson.
wazuh-event-v4.reassurance: If the event doesn’t appear, check the monitored path, configuration, time, and dashboard filter before making a second change.

wazuh-fault-v4.welcome: Let’s practice solving one small, known problem. On the practice endpoint only, we’ll briefly give the agent a wrong manager address and follow its error messages.
wazuh-fault-v4.why: This teaches us to find a connection problem from saved result instead of restarting everything and hoping it works.
needs: You’ll need a working, connected rhel9-lab-01 endpoint and its verified configuration backup.
Keep the real manager private address written down and your SSH access working.
Use only this isolated practice endpoint; never introduce this fault on a work computer.
wazuh-fault-v4.firstMove: On the endpoint, confirm the computer name and save the working agent configuration before editing it.
wazuh-fault-v4.reassurance: If you aren’t sure you can restore the working address, skip the fault for now and review the recovery step first.

wazuh-recover-v4.welcome: Let’s bring the endpoint back using the recovery method we chose earlier. We’ll check what remains afterward and prove the computer still works.
wazuh-recover-v4.why: Uninstalling software and restoring a disk do different things. A restore can also remove newer files, so we choose the branch deliberately.
needs: You’ll need the endpoint’s working starting point and the agreed recovery branch from your notes.
Keep your recovery copy and another way to reach the VM available before making changes.
Preserve any files you need and confirm whether the final goal is agent removal or restoration to the pre-install state.
wazuh-recover-v4.firstMove: Open the endpoint’s recovery record and read its chosen branch before running the package-removal example.
wazuh-recover-v4.reassurance: If your plan calls for disk restoration, don’t also run uninstall steps just because they are shown. Follow the branch that matches the recorded goal.

wazuh-close-v4.welcome: You’ve worked through the change. Let’s collect the useful saved result, say clearly what is still unfinished, and stop both lab VMs when you’re done.
wazuh-close-v4.why: Good handoff notes help the next administrator understand the result. Checking both power states also helps prevent unnecessary running costs.
needs: You’ll need the endpoint and manager results, including your event, fault, and recovery notes.
Have the Azure pages for both VMs available.
Keep private credentials separate from the redacted screenshots and notes you plan to share.
wazuh-close-v4.firstMove: Open your change record and add the final-state headings shown in the first step.
wazuh-close-v4.reassurance: An honest note about an unfinished check is more useful than writing healthy without evidence. Save what you observed and name the next action.
